content: To confirm a diagnosis of avian chlamydiosis (AC), a combination of serologic titer testing and antigen identification is required. Below are detailed descriptions of various diagnostic and treatment methods for AC: Direct Complement Fixation (CF) The direct CF test is more sensitive than agglutination methods for detecting antibodies. However, high titers may persist even after treatment, complicating the interpretation of follow-up tests. A modified version of the direct CF test offers even greater sensitivity. Elementary-Body Agglutination (EBA) The EBA test is commercially available and can detect early infections. In budgerigars, cockatiels, and lovebirds, titers greater than 10 are commonly observed in recent infections, while titers greater than 20 are seen in larger bird species. However, elevated titers may persist after treatment is completed. EBA tests, originally developed for detecting Chlamydia trachomatis in humans, are now used to identify Chlamydia psittaci in birds. These tests provide rapid results and do not require live organisms, but false positives can occur due to cross-reacting antigens, and false negatives may result from insufficient antigen presence. As with all non-culture tests, results must be interpreted alongside clinical findings. If a bird tests positive via ELISA but appears clinically healthy, the veterinarian should confirm antigen shedding through organism isolation. Immunofluorescent Antibody Tests (IFA) IFA tests use monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies, fluorescein-staining techniques, and fluorescent microscopy to identify the organism in impression smears or other specimens. These tests share similar advantages and disadvantages with ELISA. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) PCR technology is widely available for diagnostic testing. Samples such as choanal and cloacal swabs or blood can be used. However, results from unvalidated tests may be difficult to interpret. Additional Diagnostic Tests Other diagnostic techniques are either in use or under development. It is recommended to consult peer-reviewed literature before utilizing these methods. Treatment Protocols Treatment for avian chlamydiosis should be supervised by a licensed veterinarian. While current treatment protocols are generally effective, no protocol guarantees complete elimination of infection or safe treatment. Birds with AC should be treated for 45 days unless otherwise specified. Medicated Feed Medicated feed should be the sole food source during treatment. Birds’ acceptance of medicated feed varies, so food consumption must be monitored. Acceptance can be improved by first transitioning birds to a similar, non-medicated diet. Treatment begins once birds accept the medicated feed exclusively. Pellets containing 1% chlortetracycline (CTC) are suitable for most pet birds, with pellet size adjusted to the bird’s size. Special diets may be necessary for species like lories and lorikeets, which naturally consume nectar and fruit. Medicated Water Limited pharmacological studies suggest that dosages of 400 mg doxycycline hyclate per liter of water for cockatiels and 400–600 mg per liter for African grey parrots, blue-fronted Amazon parrots, and Goffin’s cockatoos maintain therapeutic concentrations. Empirical use of 400 mg per liter has been successful for many psittacine birds, excluding budgerigars. Drug toxicity can occur with this regimen, so an experienced avian veterinarian should monitor birds during treatment. Signs of toxicity include general illness (e.g., depression, inactivity, reduced appetite), green or yellow-stained urine, and altered hepatic test results (elevated aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase, and bile acids). If toxicity occurs, medication should be stopped immediately, and supportive care provided until recovery. A different treatment regimen can be initiated later. Oral Doxycycline Doxycycline is the preferred drug for oral treatment. Either the monohydrate or calcium-syrup formulations can be used. Recommended dosages are as follows: 40–50 mg/kg body weight orally once daily for cockatiels, Senegal parrots, and blue-fronted or orange-winged Amazon parrots. 25 mg/kg body weight orally once daily for African grey parrots, Goffin’s cockatoos, blue-and-gold macaws, and green-winged macaws. For other species, precise dosages cannot be extrapolated, but 25–30 mg/kg orally once daily is recommended for cockatoos and macaws, while 25–50 mg/kg orally once daily is suggested for other psittacine species. If the bird regurgitates the medication, an alternative treatment method should be used. Injectable Doxycycline Intramuscular (IM) injection into the pectoral muscle is often the easiest treatment method. However, not all injectable doxycycline formulations are suitable for IM use, and all available formulations may cause irritation at the injection site.
